subject: Mozi Minute: No half baked solutions
text:
Warren Buffet once said...

"If you get nine women pregnant, you don't have a baby in a month."

Some things just take time.

Something that Leila has taught me from an entrepreneur's perspective is patience.

Which I define as figuring out something else to do in the meantime.

That said, it's very common for us as entrepreneurs to have a problem...

-

Begin implementing a solution

-

Know that solution is going to take time to work

-

Yet, still try another thing while the other one is in the process of working

It's like having a bun half baked in the oven, and we're throwing more buns in the oven to make it go faster.

It doesn't work...

It just spreads the team and makes the original bun take longer to bake (or prevents it from doing so to begin with because the heat is too dispersed).

Rather than tell you just don't do that, here's something that has actually worked for me:

Try to find a faster feedback loop.

For example, you think to yourself:

"We're not going to know if this worked for another 90 days."

To me, that's an indication that you don't have leading indicators that are earlier on.

There's no process in a business that's going to take three months to determine whether something worked, because that means you can only do a maximum of four iterations per year.

That feedback loop is way too slow.

Although it may take 90 days to know for sure...

You should still be able to iterate on a much faster loop based on a much earlier step in whatever process you're trying to fix.

For example, if churn is a problem you're trying to fix, then a leading indicator might be activation.

Another example: if you have a super long sales cycle, an earlier activation point might be qualified calls taken with a decision-maker and budget approved.

You get the idea.

Almost any process in a business can have something that is much earlier that can validate a hypothesis (at least directionally).

That way you can try 20 improvements in the same time period that it takes your competitors to do three.

I only know this because I've done it the wrong way too.

So next time something is taking too long - ask yourself:

“Is there something earlier in the process I can iterate off?”

This is the type of stuff we work through when deconstraining a business.

Find faster feedback loops,

- Alex

subject: Mozi Minute: How I work at a computer all day with (less) pain
text:
The goal is to make it as easy as possible to work as hard as you can.

If I can help you work more, I see that as a pretty high value add.

I started seeing “pain free” as a “performance enhancer” when I realized I could work longer uninterrupted by just being more comfortable.

Context: I am a 220lb+ guy who naturally has pain after 20+ years of consistent training.

I've experimented with a lot of things, but a few of them made a significant difference in my life.

Here are four:

- To get rid of my shoulder/neck pain:

Get a desk that goes up and down. Lower your desk to sit almost on top of your lap. Almost like your hands are sitting on your lap. It being even 6 inches too high forces you to put weight on your forearms which radiates up.

- Remove your chair’s arm rests (or buy a chair without them).

Let your arms hang with weight on the palms of your hands while you type, not on your forearms. This paired with the next thing dramatically reduced my pain. I've had a bunch of my team follow suite and report the same.

- Raise your screen height.

Get a big monitor and sit it on some stacked books so that when you look straight ahead your eyes are on the middle of the screen. Your head weighs as much as a bowling ball. Having it lean even a few degrees forward all day long puts more tension on your traps and neck.

- Get a mouse that doesn't require you to turn your hand (if you have pain on your mouse hand, this is often why).

I switched from a track pad to a sideways mouse. It takes zero time to learn. So there’s no adoption curve. The goal is to make it as easy as possible to work as hard as you can.

 

If I can help you work more, I see that as a pretty high value add.

 

I started seeing “pain free” as a “performance enhancer” when I realized I could work longer uninterrupted by just being more comfortable. 

 

Context: I am a 220lb+ guy who naturally has pain after 20+ years of consistent training.

 

I've experimented with a lot of things, but a few of them made a significant difference in my life.

 

Here are four:

  1. To get rid of my shoulder/neck pain:

    Get a desk that goes up and down. Lower your desk to sit almost on top of your lap. Almost like your hands are sitting on your lap. It being even 6 inches too high forces you to put weight on your forearms which radiates up.
     
  2. Remove your chair’s arm rests (or buy a chair without them).

    Let your arms hang with weight on the palms of your hands while you type, not on your forearms. This paired with the next thing dramatically reduced my pain. I've had a bunch of my team follow suite and report the same. 

  3. Raise your screen height.

    Get a big monitor and sit it on some stacked books so that when you look straight ahead your eyes are on the middle of the screen. Your head weighs as much as a bowling ball. Having it lean even a few degrees forward all day long puts more tension on your traps and neck.

  4. Get a mouse that doesn't require you to turn your hand (if you have pain on your mouse hand, this is often why).

    I switched from a track pad to a sideways mouse. It takes zero time to learn. So there’s no adoption curve. This is the one I have. It’s great. Not affiliated. I think its ~$70. I'm sure there are cheaper ones. I don't think the brand matters. Just that it’s sideways. 

 

Give even one of them a shot and see if it helps you out.

They certainly have helped me.

I wish you maximum productivity and maximum velocity towards your future goals.

 

- Alex
